title: Scams & Fraud
description: Urgency, fake authority, and payments you cannot undo.
wolfLine: The costume changes. The hurry does not.

impostor-scam.definition: A scam where someone pretends to be a person or office you trust, such as your bank, the IRS, or a grandchild, to get money or information.
impostor-scam.example: A caller says he is from your bank’s fraud desk and asks you to move $3,000 to a “safe account.”

phishing.definition: A fake email, text, or call that pretends to be someone you trust, so you will give up a password, a code, or money.
phishing.example: A text that looks like your bank and asks you to tap a link and type your password.

lessons.title: How Scams Work
lessons.summary: The trap is the feeling, not the costume.

steps.title: Three levers
steps.body:
Most scams pull the same three levers.

Urgency: act today or lose something. Authority: they dress up as a bank, the police, or the government. Secrecy: they tell you not to check with anyone else.

steps.prompt: A text says your account closes in 15 minutes unless you tap now. Which lever is that?
choices: Urgency
Authority
Secrecy
steps.explain: The clock is the pressure. Real problems still let you hang up and check.

steps.prompt: The caller says, “I am from your bank. Do not tell your family.” Which lever is the second sentence?
choices: Secrecy
Urgency
Authority
steps.explain: Secrecy keeps you from the person who would spot the trick.

steps.prompt: A real bank will ask you to keep a problem secret from the people you trust.
steps.explain: Secrecy is the scammer’s rule, not the bank’s.

steps.prompt: A message that rushes you to act before you can think is using ___.
choices: urgency
authority
secrecy
steps.explain: Slow down. The rush is the product.

lessons.title: Phishing
lessons.summary: The logo can be copied. The link is the hook.

steps.context: [[Phishing]] is a fake email, text, or call that pretends to be someone you trust.
steps.prompt: What is phishing?
choices: A fake message that wants a password, a code, or money
Any email from a company you have never heard of
A real alert that asks you to open your bank’s app
steps.explain: The disguise is the trusted name. The goal is something only you should have.

steps.prompt: Your bank may text you to ask for your full password.
steps.explain: Banks do not ask for your password or PIN by text, email, or phone.

steps.prompt: The text uses your bank’s logo and a link. What is the careful move?
choices: Leave the link alone and open the bank’s app yourself
Tap the link so the bank can fix it
Reply with the code they asked for
steps.explain: You go to the bank. You do not let the message take you there.

steps.prompt: A link’s real job in a phishing text is to:
choices: Take you to a fake page that collects your login
Confirm your identity so the bank can protect you
Unsubscribe you from the messages
steps.explain: The page can look perfect and still belong to someone else.

steps.prompt: A correct logo means the message is safe.
steps.explain: Logos are easy to copy. The ask is what matters.

lessons.title: Spot the Fake
lessons.summary: One line gives the scam away.

steps.context: Read the whole message. The honest lines make the bad line look normal.

doc.title: Delivery notice
doc.subtitle: Text from (202) 555-0148

lines.label: Redelivery fee, pay with a gift card

totals.label: Due now to release your package

doc.note: Pay within 2 hours or your package returns to sender.

steps.prompt: Which line is the trap?
steps.explain: A surprise fee that must be paid by gift card is the hook. The real order details are the bait.

doc.title: Delivery notice
doc.subtitle: Text from (202) 555-0148

lines.label: Redelivery fee, pay with a gift card

totals.label: Due now to release your package

doc.note: Pay within 2 hours or your package returns to sender.

steps.prompt: How much is the gift-card fee they invented?
steps.explain: The redelivery line says $12.

steps.prompt: Why is a gift card a warning?
choices: Gift cards are like cash, and you cannot get them back
Gift cards take a week to clear
Carriers only take gift cards for small fees
steps.explain: Once the code is read, the money is gone.

steps.prompt: You should tap the link first, then decide.
steps.explain: The link is how the fake page gets your login.

steps.prompt: Where do you check the package instead?
choices: The store’s app, opened by you
The link in the text
A number the text tells you to call
steps.explain: You choose the door. The message does not.

lessons.title: Impostor Calls
lessons.summary: Anyone can claim a title. Hang up and call back yourself.

steps.context: An [[impostor scam|impostor-scam]] is someone pretending to be a person or office you trust: your bank, the IRS, the police, or a relative.
steps.prompt: A caller says they are the IRS and you must pay today with gift cards. What is true?
choices: The IRS does not demand gift cards over the phone
The IRS takes gift cards only for overdue bills
Paying today avoids an arrest, so it can be worth it
steps.explain: Taxes are not collected by a stranger who needs a gift card.

steps.prompt: “Your grandchild is in trouble. Do not tell their parents. Send money now.” That is a classic impostor setup.
steps.explain: Urgency, a loved one’s name, and secrecy. All three levers at once.

steps.prompt: Someone calls and says they are your bank’s fraud desk. What do you do?
choices: Hang up and call the number on your card
Give them the code that just arrived by text
Move your money where they tell you
steps.explain: The number on the card is yours to choose. Theirs is not.

steps.prompt: They already know the last four digits of your account. Does that prove they are the bank?
choices: No. Those digits leak, and scammers buy them
Yes. Only your bank can know that
Yes, if they also know your address
steps.explain: A few digits are not a secret handshake.

steps.prompt: You owe a caller an explanation before you hang up.
steps.explain: You can hang up. A real office will still be there when you call back.

lessons.title: Romance and Investment Scams
lessons.summary: Love and easy profits are the oldest bait.

steps.prompt: You have never met them, and they ask you to send money for a plane ticket. What is the careful read?
choices: This is a common romance scam
A normal step once you have talked for months
Fine, as long as they promise to pay it back
steps.explain: The relationship is the setup. The ticket is the withdrawal.

steps.prompt: An investment that “guarantees” a huge return, and punishes you for asking questions, is a warning.
steps.explain: Real investments can lose money. A guarantee plus secrecy is the tell.

steps.prompt: You already sent $500, then $500, then $500. How much is gone?
They say you must pay a “tax” before you can withdraw your profits. What is that?
choices: Another payment in the same scam
A normal fee on investment withdrawals
Proof the profits are real
steps.explain: The profits were never there. The tax is the next ask.

steps.prompt: What should you do with the chat?
choices: Stop paying and tell someone you trust
Send one more payment to unlock the rest
Keep it secret so you are not embarrassed
steps.explain: Secrecy is how the loss grows. Tell someone.

lessons.title: Gift Cards and Wires
lessons.summary: The payment method is the clue.

steps.prompt: Red flag, or an ordinary payment?
items: Pay a fee with gift cards
Wire the money today and tell no one
A bill you expected, from a company you already pay
A receipt from a store you stood in today
A stranger who will not take a normal card or bank payment
steps.explain: Gift cards, wires, and secrecy move money in a way you cannot undo.

steps.prompt: Two $200 gift cards. How much would you lose?
Why do scammers love gift cards?
choices: The code spends like cash, and the store cannot pull it back
Gift cards have the same fraud protection as a credit card
They are easy to trace back to the buyer
steps.explain: There is no refund button after the code is read.

steps.prompt: A wire to a stranger is easy to reverse the next day.
steps.explain: A wire is built to arrive and stay.

steps.prompt: A seller will only take a wire, and the deal closes tonight. What fits?
choices: Treat it as a red flag and walk away
Wire it so you do not lose the deal
Send half now as a compromise
steps.explain: A real seller can wait for a payment you can reverse.

lessons.title: The First Hour
lessons.summary: Stop the bleeding, then check the real door.

steps.context: You already know [[two-factor authentication|two-factor-authentication]]: a password plus a code.
steps.prompt: Put the first hour in order.
items: Stop. Do not send money or a login code
Call the real company on a number you look up yourself
Change the password and turn on two-factor authentication
Tell your bank if money already moved
steps.explain: Stop first. Then use a door you chose, not the one they sent.

steps.prompt: A code just arrived by text, and the caller wants it. What is it for?
choices: It lets them into the account
It proves they are the bank
It cancels the scam
steps.explain: The code is the key. Reading it aloud hands the key over.

steps.prompt: Paying “just this once” so they will stop is a good way to end it.
steps.explain: The first payment teaches them you will pay. They ask again.

steps.prompt: Money already left the account. Who do you tell first among these?
choices: Your bank or the payment app
The caller, so they can refund you
No one, until you are sure
steps.explain: The bank can sometimes freeze what is left. The caller will not.

steps.prompt: Look up the company’s number yourself. Do not use the number in the ___.
choices: message
company’s own app
back of your card
steps.explain: The message is the trap. The number you find is the exit.

lessons.title: Rosa’s Fake Delivery
lessons.summary: The fee is tiny. The card number is the prize.

story.title: The $1.99 that wasn’t
story.body:
Rosa is on her lunch break when a text arrives: her package is held for an incomplete address. To release it, tap the link and pay a **$1.99** redelivery fee within **2** hours. She did order a **$48** lamp last week.

The link opens a page with a real shipping logo and a box for her card number. Rosa closes it and opens the store’s app herself. The lamp is already on the truck.

Her coworker Jen paid the same fee last month. Two days later her card showed **$612.40** of charges she never made.

steps.prompt: What does the scammer really want from that page?
choices: Rosa’s card number
The $1.99 fee
Her home address, to deliver the lamp
why: That’s the bait. Nobody runs a scam for $1.99.
They already pretended to have that. They want something that spends.
steps.explain: The fee is small so you won’t think twice. The card number is worth far more.

steps.prompt: Jen paid $1.99 and then saw $612.40 of charges she didn’t make. How much did the text cost her in all?
Which lever is the two-hour deadline?
choices: Urgency
Authority
Secrecy
steps.explain: A clock stops you from checking.

steps.prompt: What was Rosa’s best move?
choices: Close the page and check the order in the store’s app
Pay the $1.99, since it’s too small to matter
Reply STOP to the text
why: Replying tells them the number is live. Just delete it.
steps.explain: She checked through a door she chose. The text never got a thing.

steps.prompt: Jen should call the number on the back of her card and report the charges.
steps.explain: The bank can cancel the card and dispute the charges. Card fraud is usually refunded.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Scams & Fraud
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Which ask is a scam’s favorite payment?
choices: Gift cards or a wire to a stranger
A bill you already pay each month
A debit card at the store you are standing in
steps.explain: The payment you cannot undo is the one they want.

steps.prompt: Knowing the last four digits of your account proves the caller is your bank.
steps.explain: Those digits are not a secret.

steps.prompt: A phishing text wants two $50 gift cards. How much is that?
You think a call was a scam. What is the first move?
choices: Stop, and do not read them any code
Stay on the line until they are satisfied
Send a small payment to test them
steps.explain: The code is the key. Keep it.
